subtopics.title: Historical Evolution and Gorkha Identity
subtopics.summary: The Gorkhas are people of Nepali origin, and the term is linked to the historic Gorkha Kingdom of Western Nepal. Political demands for greater autonomy trace back to the early twentieth century, and they were later voiced through a 1947 memorandum seeking Gorkhasthan and the 1980s agitation led by the Gorkha National Liberation Front. Over time, the movement increasingly articulated its objective as achieving statehood within the Indian Union.

subtopics.title: Major Bases of the Demand
subtopics.summary: Supporters argue that the Darjeeling Hills population has a distinct linguistic, cultural and social identity compared with the Bengali-majority plains. Concerns over identity insecurity and racial stereotyping have strengthened demands for stronger political recognition and representation. Economic concerns cover infrastructure, employment, developmental neglect and insufficient political and fiscal autonomy.

subtopics.title: Institutional Arrangements
subtopics.summary: Two arrangements have given the hill region a measure of autonomy. The Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council, established in 1988, was constrained by limited legislative authority, inadequate financial autonomy and dependence on the state government. The Gorkhaland Territorial Administration, established in 2011, was a more empowered autonomous arrangement with greater administrative, executive and financial responsibilities.

subtopics.title: Current Process and Challenges
subtopics.summary: The Ministry of Home Affairs recently convened a Tripartite Meeting with the Government of West Bengal and Gorkha community representatives. The Union Government then constituted a committee headed by Pankaj Kumar Singh to work out modalities for a Permanent Political Solution. The challenges include opposition to territorial division, the region's strategic location, fragmented Gorkha politics and economic sustainability.

quizzes.title: Historical Roots and Current Process
quizzes.passage: The demand for a separate political or administrative arrangement for the Nepali-speaking Gorkha population of the Darjeeling Hills in West Bengal has a long history. The Gorkhas are people of Nepali origin, and the term is linked to the historic Gorkha Kingdom of Western Nepal. Political demands for greater autonomy can be traced to the early twentieth century, when the Darjeeling Hillmen's Association petitioned during the Minto-Morley Reforms. Other organisations, including the Gorkha Officers' Association, kept raising demands for greater political autonomy in the years that followed. The Gorkhas also have a distinctive martial tradition, and the British began systematic recruitment of Gorkha soldiers after the Anglo-Nepal War. The movement became far more intense during the 1980s under a new political force. Over time, the movement's objective became clearer in its articulation. More recently, the Ministry of Home Affairs convened a Tripartite Meeting involving the Government of West Bengal and representatives of the Gorkha community. Following that meeting, the Union Government constituted a committee to work out modalities for a Permanent Political Solution. The committee will examine the issue within the Constitutional Framework, including governance arrangements and financial assistance.

quizzes.title: Institutions and Challenges Recall
quizzes.passage: Successive arrangements have tried to give the Darjeeling hill region a measure of self-governance since the agitation of the 1980s. The first such body was a hill council set up after that agitation to provide greater autonomy to the region. Its effectiveness, however, was constrained by limited legislative authority, inadequate financial autonomy and dependence on the state government. A later, more empowered autonomous arrangement was created, with greater administrative, executive and financial responsibilities than the council. Demands for a fuller political solution have nevertheless continued. Opposition in parts of the state to any further territorial division is based on concerns about territorial integrity, economic interests and administrative cohesion. The Darjeeling region also occupies a sensitive geographical position, close to three neighbouring countries. Its corridor is the main land link between mainland India and the Northeast, so prolonged instability there could have wider security implications. Gorkha politics is itself divided among several organisations and groups, which makes a common position difficult. The regional economy depends on tea, tourism and related activities, which face structural and seasonal challenges.
